newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine reforms taxed by political wrangling.
newsitem.headline: Philippine reforms taxed by political wrangling.

text.p: Manila's vaunted reforms which rescued the economy from stagnation are nearing completion but the last crucial part that deals with taxes has become bogged down in political wrangling, analysts said on Wednesday.

The government wants the comprehensive tax reform package, or CTRP, to be passed before the end of next month because only then can it bid farewell to 35 years of International Monetary Fund (IMF) supervision.
Finance Secretary Roberto de Ocampo voiced his eagerness to leave the IMF programme on schedule when he likened the Fund to a doctor whose presence made the country look like the sick man of Asia.
"We said the IMF board would complete the final review of the programme following the passage of the CTRP," IMF's Manila representative David Nellor told Reuters on Wednesday.
For the Philippines, the end of more than three decades of IMF guidance marks the graduation to the ranks of Asia's fast-growing economic stars and so usher in more investment.
Apart from casting a cloud over those hopes, squabbling by politicians over the tax bill could also jeopardise the government's financial position.

"That last part (of the tax bill) is very important. It accounts for about half of additional total revenues expected from the CTRP. If that is not passed, it would be a disaster," Peregrine Securities economist Luz Lorenzo said.
The government's total revenues are around 400 billion pesos ($15.2 billion) of which more than 80 percent comes from tax.
The CTRP, meant to reform an outmoded system that allows large-scale tax evasion, has met with opposition at every stage.
Last year, the portion dealing with "sin" taxes was delayed for months because politicians were divided between two beer firms which held opposing views on how they should be taxed.
The last part of the CTRP dealing with income tax, and currently being debated in the Senate, is a ripe source for politicking with the presidential election only a year away.
Last week, the lower house voted to grant exemption from tax to families with an annual income less than 146,000 pesos.
"That is far too high. If that goes through, we would lose revenue of around 30 billion pesos," Gil Beltran, assistant secretary for planning at the Department of Finance (DOF), said.
The Senators are less likely to go so far down the populist road and have indicated they would vote for exemption on incomes less than 96,000 pesos.

"Do we want more money in government coffers or in the pockets of consumers... some say we'd be better off if we put less money in government, which could only end up in the pockets of corrupt bureaucrats," Jose Zubiri, a member of the lower house, said.
The government's financial position has been shored up in recent years by privatisation but economists have warned this is drying up and the state needs sustainable sources of revenue.
President Fidel Ramos' government is firm on reforms and has successfully managed to push through another sensitive restructuring in which it opened up the country's oil industry.
The tax system is the last big challenge and it remains to be seen if Ramos can win once again. ($1 = 26.3 pesos)
